reading.p: The Book of Acts was written by St. Luke, the companion of St. Paul, who also wrote the Gospel of Luke. Acts is the continuation of that Gospel. It was likely written after the events recorded in Acts 28 (often placed around the 60s AD, though the exact year is debated).

Like the Gospel, Acts is addressed to Theophilus, and by extension to all catechumens and believers. Its purpose is to show how Christ continues His work through the Holy Spirit, how the Church remains one despite differences of language, culture, and persecution, and how the Gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and on to the nations.

reading.quote: It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write to you an orderly account, most excellent Theophilus...

reading.p: Luke was a physician. He is not merely telling a story; he is documenting the "case files" of how the Holy Spirit began to heal the world through the Church.

Acts is not a biography of men. It is the biography of the Holy Spirit acting through the Apostles. In the Oriental Orthodox view, the Spirit is not an abstract concept but the "Divine Energy" of God who provides the grace and power for miracles and for establishing the Church.
The Holy Spirit is not an "idea." He is God, active in the life of the Church:

reading.quote: But you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you; and you shall be My witnesses...

reading.p: Without the Holy Spirit, the Apostles are just frightened men. With the Spirit, they have the power to heal and to transform the world.

St. Peter leads the first public preaching at Pentecost and shepherds the early unity of the believers. Through the vision in Acts 10, God reveals that the "medicine and grace" of salvation is for everyone, no longer restricted by the old dietary laws or by ethnic heritage.

This was not a human innovation or a political move; it was the Holy Spirit actively guiding the "hospital" of the Church to reach more patients. Peter uses the "Keys of the Kingdom" not to lock people out but to open the doors of the Church, offering the first "diagnosis and cure"—repentance and baptism—to the thousands gathered at Pentecost.

reading.quote: But Peter, standing up with the eleven, raised his voice and said... 'Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ...'

reading.h2: The Spiritual Architect: The Holy Spirit

reading.p: In the Oriental Orthodox tradition, Acts is often called the "Gospel of the Holy Spirit." At Pentecost the Holy Spirit descends on the Apostles, transforming them from fearful men into bold witnesses. The Spirit gathers diverse nations into one body, reversing the confusion of Babel, and empowers the Apostles to perform miracles and to establish the Church.

reading.quote: They saw what seemed to be tongues of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.

...Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene; visitors from Rome (both Jews and converts to Judaism); Cretans and Arabs—we hear them declaring the wonders of God in our own tongues!
...praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily those who were being saved.

reading.p: Christ ascends, but He does not abandon the world. He reigns, and His life continues in the Church. Acts teaches that the Church is born not in a boardroom but in prayer, worship, and the "breaking of bread."
The Church grows through repentance, baptism, teaching, and the Eucharistic life. It survives through martyrdom, endurance, and unity.

reading.quote: And they continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers.
So they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for His name.

reading.h2: Structural Breakdown: The Expansion of Health

list: Acts 1-7 — The Source: The Church in Jerusalem and the martyrdom of St. Stephen.
Acts 8-12 — The Spread: The Gospel moves to Samaria and Ethiopia (the Eunuch).
Acts 13-20 — The Mission: St. Paul's three journeys, planting churches in major sees.
Acts 21-28 — The Witness: Paul's trials and his final journey to Rome.

reading.p: This is a point of great significance in our tradition. The Holy Spirit leads Philip to the Ethiopian Eunuch, a high official of Queen Candace. This fulfills the prophecy that "Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God." The Eunuch carries the "medicine" of the Gospel back to Africa before St. Paul even begins his major missions.

reading.quote: Envoys will come from Egypt; Ethiopia will quickly stretch out her hands to God.

reading.p: The Church faced external conflict in the form of persecution, prisons, and political pressure from Rome. St. Stephen, the first martyr, witnessed to the Truth even in death. There was also internal conflict—hypocrisy, ethnic tension, and leadership disputes—seen in the account of Ananias and Sapphira (integrity) and in the dispute between the Hellenists and the Hebrews (justice).

At the Jerusalem Council, the Church solved theological disputes through the Holy Spirit, maintaining unity without compromising Truth. Unity is not a loose agreement; it is a shared life in Christ. The goal is to bring all people into Tewahedo (oneness), just as St. Paul taught the Romans.

reading.h2: External Conflict: The Cost of Witness

reading.p: External conflict served as a "refiner's fire." Rather than destroying the Church, persecution often clarified its mission and spread the message further. Stephen represents the ultimate bold witness; his martyrdom proved that the grace given at Pentecost was not only for miracles but also for the courage to die for the Truth.

The Sanhedrin and Roman authorities tried to contain the movement, but the persecution in Jerusalem actually forced the believers to scatter, fulfilling the command to take the Gospel to the ends of the earth. In Exodus, God appeared in a burning bush; at Pentecost, that same Divine Fire no longer stays in a bush or a temple but rests on individuals.

Peter, who once denied Christ to a servant girl, now stands and indicts the very leaders who executed Jesus. This is not merely bravery; it is a fundamental change in his nature, an ontological change caused by the indwelling of the Spirit. The Church is not a social club but a charismatic body, fueled by the ongoing, active energy of God.

reading.h3: The Martyrdom of Stephen: The Blueprint for Courage

reading.p: Stephen was not one of the original twelve, but he was filled with Tsega (grace). His speech in Acts 7 was a direct challenge to the idea that God lived only in a building, the Temple; he argued that God moves with His people. His death proved that the Spirit's empowerment was for the sanctification of suffering, not only for success or healing. When he looked up and saw Christ standing—a sign of honor for a martyr—it changed the Church's very definition of victory.

The Sanhedrin thought that by killing Stephen and arresting leaders they would snuff out the flame. Instead of extinguishing the fire, they stepped on it and spread the sparks. These ordinary believers went to Samaria and Antioch, and political pressure forced the Church to fulfill the Great Commission.

reading.quote: And they stoned Stephen as he was calling on God and saying, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.' ... 'Lord, do not charge them with this sin.'

reading.p: St. Stephen is the first martyr. His death shows that external persecution cannot kill the Church; it only spreads the fire of the Spirit. Like Christ, he prays for his enemies, showing the ultimate health of a soul.

In Acts 5, this couple lied about their donation to the Church. The story is often misunderstood as being about money, but it was actually about spiritual counterfeit. They wanted the reputation of being generous without the sacrifice of actually being so; they were performing "holiness" for an audience.

The immediate judgment served as a kind of "quarantine." It protected the young Church from becoming a place where people could manipulate the Holy Spirit for social status, and it established that Truth is the bedrock of unity.

reading.quote: But Peter said, 'Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit... You have not lied to men but to God.'

reading.h2: Ethnic Tension and Justice (Hellenists vs. Hebrews)

reading.p: In Acts 6, Greek-speaking Jewish widows were being overlooked in favor of Hebrew-speaking ones. The Church faced a systemic issue of tribalism, as the local Hebrew-speaking Jews favored their own widows over the Hellenist ones.

The Apostles realized that prayer alone would not fix a logistics problem, so they appointed seven deacons—notably, all seven had Greek names. By giving the minority group the authority to handle the resources, they showed that unity requires justice. There can be no spiritual peace where there is physical inequality.

reading.quote: ...there arose a complaint against the Hebrews by the Hellenists... 'Therefore, brethren, seek out from among you seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom...'

reading.p: The Church did not ignore the problem; it created a structure—the Diaconate—to ensure justice. Unity requires active work and organization.

reading.h2: The Doctrine of Unity (The Jerusalem Council)

reading.p: Acts 15 records the most significant leadership dispute in the New Testament: must Gentiles become Jews and follow the Law of Moses to be saved? This was the question of legalism versus grace, the Church's first "constitutional crisis." The legalists, the Circumcision Party, argued that tradition and law were the only way to God, while Paul and Barnabas argued that the grace of the Holy Spirit was sufficient.

The Council met, debated, and listened to the Holy Spirit, arriving at a middle way: Gentiles were free from the Law but were asked to respect certain traditions to maintain fellowship with Jewish believers.

reading.quote: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us...

reading.p: They decided that the core Truth, salvation by grace, could not be compromised, but that for the sake of fellowship the Gentiles should respect certain Jewish dietary and moral laws. The lesson is that unity is not uniformity. You do not have to lose your culture, but you must share a common life and common boundaries.

reading.h2: The Apostolic Pattern: How We Grow

reading.p: Acts reveals a cycle of healing: preaching, then repentance, then baptism, then joining the life of the Church, then trial, then multiplication. In Orthodox synergy we do not merely believe with our heads; we walk in the Spirit with our whole bodies through fasting, prayer, and the sacraments.

Christianity is "physical therapy" for the soul. It requires our active participation to see results. We do not want only to be forgiven patients; we want to become transformed witnesses who help to heal others.

reading.quote: Then Peter said to them, 'Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.'

reading.p: This is the start of the cycle of healing. It begins with a change of mind (repentance) and a physical washing (baptism). You do not just feel better; you enter the treatment room.

Paul's conversion proves that the Holy Spirit can heal even the deepest "infection" of the soul. Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the Apostle, transformed from an enemy of the Church into its greatest planter and architect. No one is beyond the reach of God's grace; if the most unhealable patient can become a doctor, there is hope for everyone.

reading.quote: But the Lord said to him, 'Go, for he is a chosen vessel of Mine to bear My name before Gentiles, kings, and the children of Israel.'

reading.p: God does not merely forgive Saul; He redirects his zeal for the Gospel, making him the architect who would build the very churches he once tried to tear down. Conversion is not just a change of mind; it is a total re-making of the person by the Holy Spirit.

reading.h2: Acts 15: The Jerusalem Council and the Canon

reading.p: When conflict or confusion arises, the Church does not rely on private interpretation but meets in Council (Synod). The Apostles and elders do not vote based on politics; they discern the will of the Spirit together as one body. The Council established the "rule of life" (Canon), rules that act like a protective fence around the heart (Dogma) of our faith.

reading.quote: And as they went through the cities, they delivered to them the decrees to keep, which were determined by the apostles and elders at Jerusalem.

reading.p: Truth is found within the community of the Church, not in isolation. We stay healthy by staying obedient to the Apostolic decrees, which protect the Dogma of salvation by grace from the infection of legalism.

The Church is an organic union, not a social club. Through Apostolic Succession we are physically and spiritually connected back to the Upper Room. In Acts, the Apostles immediately chose a successor for Judas, showing that Apostolic Succession is not about paperwork but about keeping the life of the Body continuous. The Church is a living organism in which the Sacraments act as the circulatory system, pumping the life of Christ to every member.

reading.quote: Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.

reading.p: Grace is the Divine Energy that allows for Theosis. It is the medicine that does not merely mask the symptoms of sin but actually transforms the patient into the image of God.

Unity is not a natural human state; it is a gift. We must fight the sickness of division—pride, gossip, tribalism—to stay healthy in the Spirit. These three truths keep the ship of the Church steady even when the world is in a storm.

Acts ends abruptly because the mission is not over. The "Acts of the Spirit" continue today through the Sacraments and the service of the Orthodox Church. We are the current branches grafted into the Holy Root, sharing the same life force as Peter, Paul, and the Ethiopian Eunuch. We are responsible for writing the "Acts of the 21st Century" through our faith and endurance.

reading.quote: Accept one another, then, just as Christ accepted you, in order to bring praise to God.
Then Paul dwelt two whole years in his own rented house... preaching the kingdom of God and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ with all confidence, no one forbidding him.

studyGuide.overview: The Book of Acts, written by St. Luke as a continuation of his Gospel, records how the risen Christ continues His work through the Holy Spirit, spreading the Gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. It is often called the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, showing how the one Church grows through repentance, baptism, the Eucharistic life, and the witness of the martyrs.
keyPoints: Acts is the biography of the Holy Spirit acting through the Apostles, the One who empowers, sanctifies, and unites the Church.
The Gospel spreads outward from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, Ethiopia, and the nations, fulfilling Acts 1:8.
The conversion of the Ethiopian Eunuch fulfills Psalm 68:31, bringing the Gospel to Africa early in the Church's life.
The Church grows through the cycle of preaching, repentance, baptism, the common life, trial, and multiplication.
Persecution acted as a refiner's fire; the martyrdom of St. Stephen scattered believers and spread the faith.
The Jerusalem Council shows that unity is not uniformity, preserving the truth of salvation by grace while keeping fellowship.
Apostolic Succession and the Sacraments keep the life of Christ flowing continuously through the living Body of the Church.
reviewQuestions: Why is Acts called the Gospel of the Holy Spirit, and what is the Holy Spirit's role in the Church?
How does the conversion of the Ethiopian Eunuch connect to Ethiopian Orthodox tradition and to Psalm 68:31?
What are the steps in the Apostolic cycle of healing, and how do they describe Christian growth?
What did the Jerusalem Council decide, and what does it teach about unity versus uniformity?
What do the stories of Ananias and Sapphira and of the Hellenist widows teach about truth and justice in the Church?
How did persecution and the martyrdom of St. Stephen actually help the Church grow?

checks: Holy Spirit is confessed as God and as the Divine Energy/grace, consistent with Tewahedo teaching.
Procession of the Spirit is not discussed; no Filioque is implied.
Christ's reign, Ascension, and continuing life in the Church are affirmed without any Christological error.
Unity (Tewahedo/oneness), Theosis, sacraments, and Apostolic Succession presented in line with Oriental Orthodox tradition.
Veneration of St. Stephen and the martyrs framed as honor, not worship.
Ethiopian Orthodox connection (Acts 8, Psalm 68:31) drawn directly from the slides.
